title: Kestrel and the Witness
premise: Silas Voss, a meticulous night-shift dispatcher with a reputation for closing every case, is hired by an anonymous client who pays triple to prove that a murder scheduled for the solstice will never happen. The victim is real, the file is real, and the details match a cold case Silas quietly buried years ago. As Silas races a ticking statute of limitations, they discover the killer is someone inside the taxi company who has been feeding on Silas's own dispatch logs. In the end, Silas fakes the murder's success to flush the killer out, exposes their mentor as the mastermind, and chooses truth over the loyalty that once defined them — finally belonging to themselves.
about_author: Lena Hartwell is a former emergency dispatcher turned novelist who writes mysteries set in the liminal hours when cities change hands. She lives in a rain-soaked port town with a deaf cat named Alibi.

chapters.title: The Prepaid Silence
chapters.summary: Silas Voss, POV. A cash-stuffed envelope arrives at the dispatch desk with one instruction: prove that Marcus Ellery will not be murdered on the solstice. Silas, who never refuses a closed case, accepts against instinct. The beat is wary curiosity — the hook of a job that feels wrong before it even starts.

chapters.title: File 4471
chapters.summary: Silas pulls the cold case file the client referenced and freezes: the victim's details match a disappearance Silas helped misfile seven years ago. Alternating with a brief interlude from Detective Amara Okafor, who is quietly reopening the same file. The beat is dread — the past refusing to stay filed.

chapters.title: Night Shift Geography
chapters.summary: Silas maps the city through dispatch logs, tracing which drivers passed near Ellery's home on the nights that matter. The logs show a pattern too clean to be coincidence. Silas's loyalty to the company — the only family they've had — begins to chafe. The beat is creeping unease.

chapters.title: The Man Who Answers to Ellery
chapters.summary: Silas interviews Marcus Ellery, a retired coroner who seems unsurprised by the threat and oddly rehearsed. He gives Silas a partial name and a warning: 'Whoever hired you already knows how this ends.' The beat is disorientation — the client and the target may be entangled.

chapters.title: Radio Ghosts
chapters.summary: Someone replays Silas's own dispatch calls back to them over the radio, word for word, including a call Silas made off the books. Silas realizes the killer has access to the archive. The beat is violation — the watcher was inside the room all along.

chapters.title: What Ruthie Knew
chapters.summary: Silas tracks down Ruthie, a retired dispatcher and Silas's old mentor, who goes pale at File 4471 and begs Silas to let the statute run out. Flashbacks reveal the misfiled call that started everything. The beat is guilt — the case is a debt Silas owes.

chapters.title: Okafor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Detective Okafor POV. She notices the same anomalies in the dispatch logs and starts pulling threads toward the taxi company, unaware Silas is ahead of her. A near-miss at the archive leaves her suspicious of an inside hand. The beat is tightening — two investigations converging on one desk.

chapters.title: Fare Unknown
chapters.summary: Silas stakes out Ellery's street and tails a company car making an unauthorized run. The driver is clean, but the car's GPS history has been wiped by someone with supervisor access. The suspect pool shrinks to four people Silas trusts. The beat is betrayal's first taste.

chapters.title: The Solstice Ledger
chapters.summary: Silas decodes the killer's pattern: each 'murder' in the file was staged, never committed — a rehearsal for one real kill. Ellery isn't the first target; he's the last name on a list of people who covered the original crime. The beat is horror reframed — the killer is avenging, not hunting.

chapters.title: Loyalty, Itemized
chapters.summary: Silas confronts Ruthie, who admits she buried the original call to protect the company — and Silas. Silas must decide whether to turn her in or protect her as she once protected them. The beat is the theme made flesh: loyalty against truth, priced in blood.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: The dispatch office loses power on the stormiest night of the season, and the backup logs vanish. Silas, working by lantern and memory, reconstructs the missing hour and finds the killer's signature in the gaps. The beat is isolation — Silas alone with the truth, unable to prove it.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Taxi
chapters.summary: Silas lures the most likely suspect, supervisor Dean Kessler, into a night drive and records his contradictions. Kessler is hiding an affair, not a murder — a false positive that costs Silas two days. The beat is setback — the clock is now brutally short.

chapters.title: Okafor Closes In
chapters.summary: Okafor POV. She identifies the misfiled call from seven years ago and its dispatcher of record: Silas Voss. She requests an interview, polite and lethal. The beat is exposure — Silas's buried complicity surfaces at the worst possible moment.

chapters.title: The Confession Discount
chapters.summary: Silas and Okafor strike a wary bargain: Silas's old misfiling stays sealed if they deliver the killer before the statute expires. They pool files and realize the killer's knowledge of dispatch procedure is expert-level. The beat is reluctant alliance — two loners learning to share the load.

chapters.title: Four Names, Three Alibis
chapters.summary: The suspect pool narrows again, and the only person left with archive access and no alibi is someone Silas refuses to suspect: the night manager who trained them, Wren Halloway. The beat is denial — Silas defending the last loyalty they have left.

chapters.title: Ellery's Last Fare
chapters.summary: Ellery disappears two days before the solstice. His apartment holds a staged scene, complete with the killer's signature — but no body. Silas realizes the killer is rehearsing the final murder early, and Ellery may still be alive. The beat is urgency spiked with hope.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Silas and Okafor stake out the company archive, betting the killer will return to alter the last log. A figure arrives; the chase fails, but a dropped keycard points to Wren. The beat is confirmation shadowed by grief — the mentor is the monster.

chapters.title: What Wren Taught Me
chapters.summary: Silas confronts Wren, who confesses with terrifying calm: the original victim was her sister, and every 'murder' since was her making the record tell the truth the law refused to. She asks Silas to let Ellery die — the last name on the cover-up. The beat is devastating empathy — the killer is the person who made Silas.

chapters.title: The Statute and the Storm
chapters.summary: With hours left, Silas devises a trap: broadcast a fake log showing Ellery 'found safe' elsewhere, forcing Wren to move him before the statute lapses. Okafor objects to the risk; Silas stakes their career and freedom on it. The beat is resolve — truth weaponized at last.

chapters.title: Solstice
chapters.summary: The trap springs at the abandoned depot where the original call was made. Wren takes Ellery to the edge and stops — because Silas, on the radio, reads the original dispatch call aloud, finally putting the truth on the record. Wren surrenders to the voice, not the police. The beat is climax as catharsis — truth as the only mercy left.

chapters.title: Closing the Case
chapters.summary: Fallout: Wren is charged, Ruthie turns herself in, and Silas's sealed misfiling comes out anyway — costing them the job but not Okafor's respect. Silas testifies, unflinching, choosing truth over the family that lied for them. The beat is cost and clarity — belonging rebuilt on honest ground.

chapters.title: Open Channel
chapters.summary: Months later, Silas runs a small independent dispatch service, the radio quiet, the city gentler at night. A new envelope arrives — prepaid, anonymous, one line: 'I know something you don't.' Silas smiles, picks up the pen, and opens a fresh file. The beat is renewal — the case-closer, changed, answering the call again.
